newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Hungry LUKoil bids to be top Russian share.
newsitem.headline: Hungry LUKoil bids to be top Russian share.

text.p: Russia's largest oil producer and reform success story LUKoil will consider new ways to feed its hunger for expansion and bolster its bid to become Russia's premier company at its annual meeting on Thursday.
Shareholders may authorise issuing 10 million new preferred shares worth $110 million at current market rates that the board of directors intends to use in gas and oil acquisitions.
Vertically integrated LUKoil Holding has leapt ahead of its competitors, consolidating shares of subsidiary companies. But it says profit growth will slow as it prepares for long-term growth.

The firm's annual report forecasts 1997 net profit will rise to 4.0-4.5 trillion roubles from 3.87 trillion in 1996, to Russian cash accounting standards, but sales will jump to 55-60 trillion roubles from 43.99 trillion.
"We think that 1997 could be called the investment year," spokesman Pytor Neyev said recently.
Some analysts question whether LUKoil investment policy should have such a strong impact on its bottom line.
Despite LUKoil's Formula One sponsorship and Western-style gasoline station chain, many see the firm as Russia's best company -- but not the equivalent of a U.S. major.
United City Bank research director Christopher Granville picked out LUKoil as an example of the murky finances among top companies, with a few different figures for 1996 net income.
"It is perfectly clear that the real picture is being disguised," he told a conference.
Analysts disagree whether LUKoil, trading at $15.30 on Wednesday on the Russian Trading System, up from $6.20 last April, is overvalued.

The preferred share authorisation could be considered a dilution of existing holdings, since it will not be offered to current shareholders. But LUKoil says this is not the case because it will be used for new acquisitions.
A Western analyst at a Moscow brokerage said LUKoil, the largest oil company on the Russian equity market, was a unique type of investment.

"In the oil industry you have two ways of investing today," he said. "You either buy LUKoil, a transparent, high-quality, long-term company. Or you buy a speculative second tier, betting on merger terms between production and holding companies."
Lukoil's $11 billion valuation is one-eighth of total Russian stock market capitalisation.

Most Russian oil holdings are still consolidating their production and holding units. The two trade separately -- and typically only the production company has much market liquidity in Russia -- and it is in the interest of the holding company to deflate production company prices to make consolidation cheaper.
LUKoil is also ahead of its peers seeking Western capital.
Securities director Leonid Fedun says LUKoil wants to offer several investment options to increase liquidity. "The larger the market, the larger the circle of investors," he said.

Investors snapped up a $200 million LUKoil convertible bond issue in April and LUKoil plans to sell about 15 percent of shares in a global offering, probably early next year and is also considering a Eurobond for 1998.

LUKoil has formed a $5 billion joint venture with Atlantic Richfield Co , which has an eight percent strategic stake in the company, and is active in Kazakhstan and Iraq as well as taking a stake in the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which will transport oil from rich Central Asian fields to the West.
"If you assume nothing is going to happen to LUKoil, (it is fairly valued)," said the Western analyst. "But there is expansion on all fronts."
--Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
